title: Partial Prerendering and Cache Components
summary: Combine a fast prerendered page shell with dynamic regions that resolve when a request arrives.

subtopics.title: Separate shared and changing content
subtopics.explanation: Shared content, such as navigation or a product description, may be prepared before a visit. User-specific details or current stock may require request-time work. Mark which parts can safely be reused. It is like setting the table before knowing which meal a guest orders.

subtopics.title: Build the shell
subtopics.explanation: The framework can render content that does not need request-time information into an initial shell. The shell should already help the visitor understand the page and available actions.

subtopics.title: Defer dynamic work
subtopics.explanation: Wrap request-time work in a Suspense boundary with a fallback. The framework can include that fallback in the shell while dynamic content waits. Keep the boundary close to the work so unrelated content can appear sooner.

subtopics.title: Stream ready content
subtopics.explanation: As dynamic regions become ready, the server can stream their content into the page. Independent regions may resolve at different times. Make each region understandable while it is loading or unavailable.

subtopics.title: Use current Next.js configuration
subtopics.explanation: Current Next.js documentation describes this model through Cache Components and the cacheComponents configuration. Older releases used experimental settings. Check the installed Next.js version and deployment support instead of copying old configuration.

foundations.overview: Some page content is shared and can be prepared before a visit. Other content depends on a request, such as a signed-in user or current inventory. Partial Prerendering combines those parts: the browser can receive a useful shell while dynamic regions wait. In current Next.js, Cache Components provides this model when enabled; learn the version-specific configuration before applying it.
foundations.mentalModel: A restaurant can bring the menu first while a made-to-order dish is prepared.
foundations.whyItMatters: A page can show shared content quickly without pretending personalized or changing data is already available.
foundations.formalDefinition: Partial Prerendering separates content that can be prerendered from dynamic content that resolves at request time and streams into defined boundaries.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser receives the prerendered shell and fallback UI, then updates dynamic regions as streamed content arrives.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use Suspense boundaries around request-time data and check the Cache Components requirements for the Next.js version in use.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Keep dynamic work inside deliberate boundaries and provide useful fallbacks.
foundations.performanceImpact: More static shell content can arrive early; poorly placed boundaries can delay useful content.
commonUseCases: Dashboards with shared navigation and private data
Pages mixing static descriptions with request-time recommendations

commonMisconceptions.myth: PPR means every page is automatically static and dynamic at once
commonMisconceptions.reality: The framework needs clear boundaries and version-appropriate configuration for dynamic work.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A fallback is only a spinner
commonMisconceptions.reality: A good fallback preserves page structure and explains what information is still loading.

keyTakeaways: Keep shared content in the prerendered shell where it is safe.
Use Suspense boundaries and useful fallbacks for dynamic regions.
Follow the Cache Components setup for your installed Next.js version.
